sections.h2: What kind of county is Brantley County, Georgia?
sections.html:
Brantley County is a rural county in southeast Georgia with its seat at Nahunta. It covers about 442 square miles of land, and the Satilla River runs through it, according to Wikipedia. Georgia voters approved the county's creation on November 2, 1920, carving it from parts of Charlton, Pierce and Wayne counties.

The 2020 census counted 18,021 people, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 18,936. The same source lists 8,537 housing units, a median owner-occupied home value of $99,600 and an owner-occupied rate of 79.9 percent for 2020 to 2024 (Census QuickFacts). Only 77 building permits were recorded for 2025, so the housing stock turns over slowly and most sellers are long-time owners of single-family homes, acreage or mobile homes.

sections.h2: Which Brantley County offices deal with property tax?
sections.html:
Two offices share the Brantley County Government Annex at 10405 Main Street North in Nahunta: the tax commissioner bills and collects, and the tax assessor values property. Neither office sets the tax rate. The rate comes from the county commissioners and the school board.

The county's tax offices page lists both numbers, and the commissioner's own site at brantleytax.com and the assessor's site at qpublic.net give the details below.

sections.h2: What does the Brantley County tax commissioner bill?
sections.html:
The commissioner's office bills and collects ad valorem taxes on several kinds of property. Per its website, those are:

  • Real property, meaning land and buildings
  • Personal property
  • Motor vehicles
  • Mobile homes
  • Timber

You can search any parcel and pay online through the same site. The site's news page carries tax sale notices, a list of excess funds and the office's holiday closings. Check it before you list a home that has unpaid years on it, because a parcel that goes to tax sale becomes much harder to sell on the open market.

The due date for the annual bill is printed on the bill itself. If you cannot find yours, call 912-462-5723 and ask for the due date and a payoff figure.

Keep a printout of the paid receipt for every year you own the property. A buyer's title company will ask for proof that earlier years are clear, and a receipt from the commissioner's office settles the question quickly.

sections.h2: How are homes valued in Brantley County?
sections.html:
The assessor's office says it updated all its schedules in 2025 and ran a complete re-evaluation of every property. It maintains records for 13,406 real property parcels, 602 personal property accounts and 2,346 mobile homes that do not carry a homestead exemption.

Georgia assesses property at 40 percent of fair market value as of January 1. The assessor's site tells owners that tax returns are due between January 1 and April 1. If you skip the return, assessment notices are mailed in the middle of May, and that notice starts your appeal clock.

  • File a return by April 1 if you want to state your own value.
  • Read the notice the day it arrives and note the date printed on it.
  • Call the assessor at 912-462-5251 with questions before the window closes.

Because the re-evaluation changed values across the county, a home that looked cheap on paper a few years ago may now carry a noticeably different assessment. Pull the current record before you set a sale price.

If you plan to sell within the year, compare your own record against recent sales in the county. A record that lists the wrong square footage, an old outbuilding or a missing improvement is easier to correct before a buyer's appraiser notices it.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Brantley County assessment?
sections.html:
You have 45 days from the date on the assessment notice to appeal, and the assessor's site warns that this is the only window. The appeal goes first to the Board of Tax Assessors, and Georgia's usual path then runs to the county Board of Equalization and finally to Superior Court, with arbitration offered as an alternative to the board hearing.

Appeal on value, uniformity or taxability. A complaint that the bill is too large does not qualify, because the bill depends on the millage rate, which is not appealable.

  • Put the appeal in writing and keep a copy.
  • Bring recent sales of similar homes nearby and any repair estimates.
  • Ask the assessor how to request a hearing.

The 45-day count starts on the notice date, not on the day you open the envelope, so a late mailbox check can eat into your time.

sections.h2: What do Brantley County's housing numbers mean for a seller?
sections.html:
The county is thinly settled, with about 40.7 people per square mile in 2020 and 99.3 percent of residents living in rural areas. Buyers here are mostly local, and many homes sit on large lots or come with mobile home placements. Households number 6,599 for 2020 to 2024, and 94.3 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so listings are scarce and long ownership is the norm (Census QuickFacts).

Median gross rent is $755 and median owner costs with a mortgage run $1,087 a month, both the lowest of the four counties on that table. Three practical points follow for an owner thinking about a sale:

  • Many owners hold inherited or family land, so confirm who is on the deed and who is on the tax bill before you list.
  • Brantley is part of the Brunswick metropolitan area, and Wayne, Glynn, Camden, Charlton, Ware and Pierce counties touch it, so buyers often compare it with those neighbors.
  • Roughly one in five residents is 65 or older, which makes estate and heir questions common. Ask the probate court about your situation if the owner has died.

sections.h2: What should a Brantley County seller do about tax owed at closing?
sections.html:
Start with a payoff figure from the tax commissioner, because unpaid county taxes have to be cleared for the buyer to get clean title. Ask the closing attorney or title company how the current year's bill will be split between you and the buyer.

If the house is a mobile home, confirm whether it is billed on its own or together with the land, since the assessor tracks non-homesteaded mobile homes as separate accounts. Homestead status affects this, so ask the assessor which treatment your home has.

Owners affected by the Highway 82 fire can reach the county commissioners' office at 912-462-5256, extension 5, for recovery resources listed on the county website. Ask the assessor how fire damage is reflected in your record before you price the property.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in Brantley County?
faqs.a: Pay the tax commissioner, either online through brantleytax.com or at the Government Annex, 10405 Main Street North, Suite D, Nahunta. The office phone is 912-462-5723, and hours are 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday to Friday.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Brantley County assessment?
faqs.a: You have 45 days from the date printed on the assessment notice. The assessor's website says this window is firm, so file in writing before it closes.

faqs.q: Does the Brantley County assessor set my tax bill?
faqs.a: No. The assessor sets the value only. The county commissioners and the school board set millage rates, and the tax commissioner sends the bill.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Brantley County house if taxes are unpaid?
faqs.a: Yes, but the back taxes must be paid at or before closing so the buyer receives clear title. Call the tax commissioner for a payoff and have the closing attorney include it on the settlement statement.

faqs.q: When are Brantley County property tax returns due?
faqs.a: Returns are due between January 1 and April 1 each year. If you miss that deadline, assessment notices are mailed in the middle of May and the 45-day appeal period begins.
